case_study_insert.main_stem: Ashcombe Eco Bricks (AEB) is a private limited company in the building materials sector, employing a workforce of 140. Founded in 1998 by Marta Ashcombe, the business manufactures recycled-content eco blocks and facing blocks for the housebuilding market and operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. AEB plans to invest $980,000 in a new recycled-aggregate batching plant and vibro-compaction press, financed by hire purchase, a $550,000 bank loan and $430,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $888,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.80 a unit and a selling price of $8.50, and currently produces 305,000 units a year. AEB faces two operational problems: absenteeism has reached 11% and recycled-aggregate inconsistency is causing occasional sub-standard batches.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Sales Report — Q3 2025: The batching plant produced 84,000 blocks in the quarter at a sub-standard batch rate of 1.6%, down from 2.7% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 25 to 11 per month. Market research of 420 housebuilders found that 69% specify recycled-content blocks and 61% would pay up to $0.80 more per block. Average delivery time is 3 days, and dust-control upgrades costing $35,000 are scheduled for winter. Average strength of blocks is 7.3 N/mm².

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Ashcombe Eco Bricks for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, the third rise this year, raising variable-rate borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.7% from $12.60 to $13.44 per hour from April 2026, materially raising wage bills. (3) Cement and recycled aggregate input costs have risen 7.6% year-on-year, while housing construction output grew 2.4% and building-materials inflation is running at 6.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: AEB plans to acquire its new vibro-compaction press by hire purchase. Explain two advantages for AEB of using hire purchase for the press instead of a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $980,000 cost of the batching plant and vibro-compaction press into fixed instalments without an immediate capital outlay, easing cash flow while AEB already carries fixed costs of $888,000 a year and services a $550,000 bank loan. Crucially, ownership passes to AEB once the final payment is made, so the press becomes a long-term asset producing 305,000 units a year without the flat structure straining to raise or secure a larger unsecured facility.

Point 2: Hire purchase keeps the specific press asset as security for the finance provider rather than general charges over AEB's premises or other equipment, protecting Marta Ashcombe's flexibility to mortgage land later if the eco-block range expands. It also matches payments to output: as the recycled-content blocks generate revenue at $8.50 a unit, instalments track productive use, and AEB keeps $430,000 of retained profit in reserve for the $35,000 dust-control upgrades and for materials during aggregate-price spikes.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Ashcombe Eco Bricks and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: AEB is launching its recycled-content eco blocks. Consider local radio sponsorship, builders' merchant in-store promotion, or a social media campaign targeting self-build homeowners. Which should AEB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio sponsorship: Sponsoring a local home-and-garden show would reach self-build homeowners across AEB's distribution radius cheaply and with high frequency, reinforcing the family-firm brand founded by Marta Ashcombe in 1998. Its weaknesses are narrow reach beyond the region, difficulty communicating technical benefits such as 7.3 N/mm² strength, and no targeting of the 69% of professional housebuilders who specify recycled-content blocks — most radio listeners are private individuals, not AEB's core trade customers.

Builders' merchant in-store promotion: Stands, leaflets, staff briefings and demonstration samples inside merchants put the product in front of trade buyers at the exact point of specification and purchase — reaching the 61% willing to pay $0.80 more per block. It is tactile and persuasive, but depends on merchant goodwill and staff effort, competes with rival brands for counter space, and cannot build mass awareness outside the merchant network.

Social media campaign targeting self-build homeowners: Content on recycled aggregate, carbon savings and strength tests reaches a fast-growing DIY audience directly, at low cost, with measurable engagement — ideal for driving them into merchants asking for AEB blocks. However, self-builders are a minority of volume demand; housebuilders still drive most of the 305,000-unit output, and social content requires ongoing budget and creative to stay fresh.

Recommendation: AEB should choose builders' merchant in-store promotion supported by light social media. The merchant channel reaches the professional buyers who specify blocks on every housing estate — the 69% specifying recycled content — at the moment of purchase, and reinforces AEB's 3-day delivery promise. Local radio is rejected as too narrow and untargeted for trade demand; a pure social campaign is rejected as consumer-facing reach that does not guarantee specification; in-store plus digital proof (QR codes linking to test certificates) should convert interest at the counter.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of AEB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of AEB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and pure social are rejected.

questions.question_text: AEB's absenteeism has reached 11%. Explain two advantages for AEB of introducing a bonus scheme linked to block output for its machine operators.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: An output-linked bonus gives each of AEB's 140 machine operators a direct financial stake in hitting the 84,000 blocks produced last quarter and the 305,000-unit annual target, satisfying a basic financial motivator (Herzberg) on top of the flat autocratic supervision. Operators who earn more when the vibro-compaction press runs well are more likely to attend reliably, attacking the 11% absenteeism and reducing the overtime needed to cover absences.

Point 2: Output bonuses reward the operators who reduce the 1.6% sub-standard batch rate and keep recycled aggregate consistent, because consistent batches mean more saleable blocks per shift. Higher pay for good attendance and clean batches lowers unit labour cost against the $4.80 variable cost, supports the $8.50 selling price, and reinforces Marta Ashcombe's autocratic cost-discipline culture — though it must be paired with quality checks so speed never outruns the 7.3 N/mm² strength standard.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AEB's absenteeism, output, quality and costs.

questions.question_text: AEB must choose its production method for the new eco blocks. Consider flow production or batch production. Which should AEB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Flow production: A continuous line through batching, vibro-compaction, curing and packing would slash unit costs, spread the $980,000 fixed investment over maximum volume, minimise handling damage — helping hold strength at 7.3 N/mm² — and deliver the 3-day delivery promise consistently. It suits the standardised eco block that the 69% of specifying housebuilders want in repeat, identical quantities, and maximises the 305,000-unit annual output. Its weaknesses are inflexibility: any change to block size, facing mix or aggregate specification stops the whole line, and a breakdown idles the entire plant.

Batch production: Producing in batches lets AEB switch between eco blocks, facing blocks and specialist shapes (retaining units, lintel packs), using the same batching plant flexibly — valuable while aggregate consistency causes 1.6% sub-standard batches, as suspect batches can be isolated and rejected without scrapping a whole continuous run. Unit costs are higher and changeover times add waste, but it suits AEB's variable order pattern from housebuilders and reduces risk during commissioning of the new press.

Decision: AEB should choose flow production for its core eco block, with a small batch-production cell retained for specialist products. The core range is standardised, demand from housebuilders is repeatable, and flow production gives the lowest unit cost and best route to dilute the $980,000 investment — rejected batch production as the main method because it would raise handling, changeover and unit costs precisely when input inflation is 7.6%. Batch flexibility stays as insurance for specification variety and for quarantining sub-standard aggregate without losing a shift's output.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two production methods with limited application to AEB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both production methods in the context of AEB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both production methods in the context of AEB with a well-justified decision covering cost, flexibility, quality and delivery.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how AEB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $888,000 ÷ ($8.50 − $4.80) = $888,000 ÷ $3.70 = 240,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 240,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $8.50 − $4.80 = $3.70. Answer: contribution per unit is $3.70.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways AEB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. AEB's managers can compare the 240,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 305,000 units, confirming a margin of safety of 65,000 units, and decide whether to push the vibro-compaction press harder during peak housebuilding seasons.
2. Contribution per unit of $3.70 lets managers model a 61% majority-premium price rise of $0.80, lifting contribution to $4.50, and judge whether the premium can be charged without losing specifying housebuilders.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $888,000 and contribution per unit helps managers test whether the $980,000 investment pays back through incremental units, and set the volume targets needed to service hire purchase instalments and the $550,000 bank loan.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($888,000 ÷ 305,000 units + $4.80 = $7.71 a unit) to benchmark performance across quarters, pinpoint the recycled-aggregate inconsistency driving the 1.6% sub-standard batches, and decide whether to renegotiate the $4.80 variable cost with aggregate suppliers amid the 7.6% input-cost rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 240,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $3.70 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 65,000 units against 305,000-unit output; $0.80 premium modelling against $888,000 fixed costs; affordability testing for the $980,000 investment against the $550,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $7.71 to tackle 1.6% sub-standard batches and aggregate inconsistency.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate AEB's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has AEB's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 45.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 47.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 14.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 24.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $5,200,000 revenue − $2,860,000 cost of sales = $2,340,000; 2025 gross profit = $6,000,000 − $3,180,000 = $2,820,000. 2024 operating profit of $650,000 ÷ revenue of $5,200,000 = 12.5%; 2025 operating profit of $840,000 ÷ revenue of $6,000,000 = 14.0%. 2024 operating profit of $650,000 ÷ capital employed of $3,250,000 = 20.0%; 2025 operating profit of $840,000 ÷ capital employed of $3,500,000 = 24.0%. Revenue grew $800,000 while cost of sales grew just $320,000, so gross profit rose $480,000.

Evaluation: Profitability has improved, and efficiently. The gross margin edged up to 47.0% on the strength of recycled-content specification and tighter aggregate control — evidenced by sub-standard batches falling to 1.6%. Operating profit rose 29% to $840,000 on revenue growth of about 15%, showing genuine operating leverage after the batching-plant investment. Capital employed grew just $250,000, so returns on that capital jumped to 24.0%, comfortably covering the $135,000 interest payable on the $550,000 loan. Risks remain: the 7.6% cement and aggregate inflation could cut the gross margin in 2026, and 11% absenteeism adds overtime and quality risk that could erode the 14.0% operating margin if not fixed through the planned bonus scheme.

Conclusion: AEB's profitability has improved. Gross profit, operating profit and the return on capital employed all rose in 2025, and the improvement was achieved without a proportionate rise in capital employed — a genuinely efficient expansion. To sustain it, AEB must lock in aggregate contracts, hold the dust-control and absenteeism programmes to target, and protect the $0.80 certified premium at the point of sale.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether AEB's profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for AEB of producing recycled-content eco blocks instead of standard concrete blocks.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled-content blocks match the 69% of 420 surveyed housebuilders specifying recycled content and the 61% willing to pay up to $0.80 more per block, letting AEB charge a premium that protects its $3.70 contribution per unit even as cement and aggregate input costs rise 7.6%. It also strengthens AEB's environmental brand — diverting demolition waste from landfill — which supports inclusion in housebuilders' sustainable supply-chain frameworks and justifies the $980,000 batching-plant investment.

Disadvantage: Recycled aggregate varies in size, contamination and moisture, which is exactly why AEB suffers occasional sub-standard batches at 1.6% and needs the 7.3 N/mm² strength standard policed. If aggregate consistency worsens, AEB risks failing strength tests, breaching merchant listings or facing claims, while the extra sorting and washing raise the $4.80 variable cost — squeezing margins if the $0.80 premium is not accepted across the whole range.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AEB's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.7% minimum wage increase and the 7.6% rise in cement and recycled aggregate input costs will affect AEB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.25%): On AEB's $550,000 bank loan, a 0.50 percentage point rise adds roughly $2,750 a year — trivial beside fixed costs of $888,000. Higher rates may cool housebuilding finance and slow the 2.4% growth in construction output, trimming orders, and raise the cost of future borrowing; AEB could fix rates at renewal to neutralise this.

Minimum wage increase (6.7%, to $13.44 per hour): AEB employs 140 staff, mostly machine operators and yard crew on or near the minimum wage. The rise adds about $0.84 an hour, roughly $1,750 per worker a year — around $245,000 across the workforce if applied to all 140. That is nearly 29% of 2025 operating profit of $840,000 and would land on top of 11% absenteeism, making attendance management and the planned output-linked bonus essential to protect margins; it is a severe, recurring cash drain regardless of volume.

Input cost inflation (7.6% cement and recycled aggregate): Materials make up roughly 65% of the $4.80 variable cost (about $3.12). A 7.6% rise adds about $0.24 per unit; at 305,000 units that is roughly $73,000 a year. AEB can recover much of this through the $0.80 certified premium and housebuilder price reviews, and has aggregate contracts to renegotiate — but partial recovery is the realistic ceiling this year.

Conclusion: The 6.7% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 140 employees whatever happens to sales volume, adding roughly $245,000 a year — more than three times the input-cost rise and nearly ninety times the loan interest increase — and it strikes the labour-heavy part of the process hardest. Input costs (~$73,000) are the second-greatest threat and are partly recoverable through price reviews; the rate rise is the smallest and most easily hedged, though all three demand AEB prioritise attendance, productivity and premium pricing to defend its margins through 2027.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to AEB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on AEB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of AEB with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
